analysis.one_liner: Requires stronger federal safety standards for car seat backs to protect crash occupants.
analysis.headline: A bill to update seat back strength standards that NHTSA has not revised in more than 50 years died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a vote, never leaving committee in the two-year Congress with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to rewrite federal motor vehicle safety standard 571.207, the rule governing how strongly a car seat must hold up in a crash, and required automakers to comply within two model years of the rule taking effect. The bill's findings say the standard has not been meaningfully updated in more than 50 years and lists named victims of seat back failures, particularly children riding in rear seats. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in cars, especially children and other rear-seat passengers, whose seats are the most likely to fail in a rear-impact crash. The bill's findings cite thousands of preventable deaths and life-threatening injuries from seat failures and name individual victims of seat back collapse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car passengers, especially children in back seats

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Transportation to issue a final rule updating federal seat integrity standard 571.207 to reduce injury from seat back failure in all types of vehicle impact.

The bill's findings state that crashes involving seat structural failures pose a significant threat to occupants, particularly children in rear seats, and that thousands of preventable fatalities and life-threatening injuries have resulted from seat failures.
The findings state that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has not improved the seat integrity standard for more than 50 years.
Requires a compliance deadline no later than two motor vehicle model years after the rule takes effect, so the stronger standard reaches new cars quickly rather than being deferred indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of engineering and testing stronger seats, with some of that cost passed to new-car buyers through vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to all motor vehicle seating systems and requires compliance within two model years of the rule, so automakers would bear redesign, testing, and certification costs on a fixed timeline, some of which would likely be passed on to consumers in vehicle prices.

The bill requires a final rule within two years of enactment, a short timeline for a safety rule that would normally go through notice, comment, and testing standards, which industry could have argued risks a rushed or technically flawed standard.

The bill gives the Secretary of Transportation discretion over the technical content of the new standard beyond the directive to reduce injury from seat back failure, leaving the actual cost and design changes to be determined by rulemaking rather than by Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a reduction in deaths and catastrophic injuries, chiefly among rear-seat passengers and children, from a failure mode the bill says has gone unaddressed for more than half a century. The cost is engineering and price impact borne by automakers and spread across new-car buyers, on the same model as existing federal vehicle safety standards. The design is straightforward and the cost is the normal cost of a safety mandate; the main weakness is the compressed two-year rulemaking deadline.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2021, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, joined by Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The only additional cosponsor recorded was Sen. Blumenthal.
No further action appears in the bill's history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because no compliance deadline for stronger seats was ever set, and current seat strength requirements remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, who face no new seat mandate

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing DOT to update the seat back safety standard and named crash victims of seat failures in its findings.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Her committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after referral in April 2021 the bill's action history shows no further committee action through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and only the two Democratic senators signed on, so there is no record of how other members would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would have required redesigned, stronger seats within two model years of a new DOT rule, a compliance cost automakers would have avoided by the bill's failure. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate runs against occupant safety, particularly for rear-seat passengers.
A revised seat integrity standard would have forced reengineering of seating systems sold to automakers. The bill's death leaves current seat design requirements in place.

industries.industry: Car buyers and crash victims' families
industries.note: Occupants would have gained from a modernized seat strength standard; the bill specifically cites children in rear seats as the most exposed group. Families of named victims supported stronger standards through the bill's findings.
